title: Wildcard Matching
prompt: Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p`, implement wildcard pattern matching that supports `?` and `*`, where `?` matches any single character and `*` matches any sequence of characters, including the empty sequence. The matching must cover the entire input string, not just part of it.

examples.explanation: "a" does not match the entire string "aa".
'?' matches 'c', but the second letter is 'a' in p while it's 'b' in s.

constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters
p consists of only lowercase English letters, '?', or '*'
hints: Unlike regex '*', here '*' stands alone and can match any sequence of any length (including empty) by itself — no preceding character to repeat.
Define dp[i][j] = true if s[0:i] matches p[0:j]. If p[j-1] is '*', it can either match zero characters (dp[i][j-1]) or absorb one more character of s while still being available (dp[i-1][j]).
If p[j-1] is '?' or matches s[i-1] exactly, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. Base case: dp[0][j] is true only if p[0:j] is made entirely of '*' characters, since only '*' can match an empty string.

solution.approach: Define dp[i][j] as true if s[0:i] matches p[0:j]. dp[0][0] = True (empty matches empty). dp[0][j] is true only while p[0:j] consists entirely of '*' so far, since that's the only character able to match an empty remaining string. For general cells, if p[j-1] is '?' or exactly equals s[i-1], the match reduces to whether the prefixes before them matched: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. If p[j-1] is '*', it can match zero characters of s (dp[i][j-1], leaving the '*' unused) or it can absorb one more character of s while remaining available to absorb more (dp[i-1][j]) — either possibility being true makes dp[i][j] true, since '*' greedily covers any length. The answer is dp[len(s)][len(p)].
